levels.name: Word
levels.description: Reading words of increasing length fluently and combining them into simple sentences.

data.instruction: Two-letter words are short but important. Build each one, then try reading it without help.
Three-letter words often follow a consonant-vowel-consonant pattern. Build each word.
Four-letter words may include a blend or a silent letter. Take your time building each one.
Five-letter words are longer, but the same blending skills apply. Build each one carefully.
Sight words don't always follow normal sound rules, so it helps to recognize them by sight. Practice each one.

data.title: The Ant and the Grasshopper
data.text: One day, the grasshopper was hoping and singing in the field. An ant passed by carrying an ear of maize. The grasshopper called him to play but he said he was preparing for the dry season. The grasshopper did not seem to worry. When the drought came, ant had enough for himself. The grasshopper got a little share from the ant.
data.teaser: What do you think this story teaches about planning ahead?

questions.question: Why did the ant refuse to play with the grasshopper?

data.title: A Lion and the Rat
data.text: The lion had just finished his meal. He was resting under a shade. Suddenly, a rat decided to play on his face. The lion caught the rat and wanted to eat him. The rat begged him to save his life. The lion decided to let him go. One day, the lion fell into a hunter's trap. He roared in anger. The whole forest could hear him. The rat knew it was time to return the favor. Before the hunters came back, the rat ate up the trap and the lion was free. He thanked the grateful rat.
data.teaser: Do you think small acts of kindness can come back to help you later?

questions.question: How did the rat save the lion?
options: By eating through the trap to free him
By roaring to scare the hunters
By hiding the lion in a hole

data.title: Zeke the Zebra
data.text: Zeke lives in the savannah. Here, grasses are tall with very few trees and no mountains. There is a river from which all the animals in the savannah drink. Most of these animals are Zeke's friends. Though Zeke is a zebra, he always wanted to look like other animals. He admired how swift the horse was and wished for long hairs. He adored the big flappy ears of the elephant. How he wished he could walk on two legs. When he learnt that he could not have all these, he is happy with himself.
data.teaser: Why do you think it's important to be happy with who you are?

questions.question: What did Zeke admire about the elephant?

data.title: The Magical Honey Pot
data.text: One morning, the bear was looking for his honey pot. He looked for it under his bed and could not find it. He looked for it on his bookshelf but it was not there. The bear called his friend rabbit. He asked rabbit to help him find the honey pot. They looked all over but could not find it. Suddenly, rabbit saw something drop from the roof. It was bear's honey pot. Luckily, it did not break. They were both very happy. From that day on, bear calls it the magical honey pot.
data.teaser: Where do you think the honey pot had been hiding the whole time?

questions.question: Where did rabbit finally spot the honey pot?

data.title: Peter's Fortune
data.text: There was a big tree in the garden, just a few steps from the window. Peter decided to cut down the tree. A woodcutter came and cut the tree. The roots were widely spread. The woodcutter had to dig a big hole. He suggested that the hole could be used as a rubbish pit. Peter climbed down and saw some gold coins. Next to the coins, he saw a green metal box. It had rings, necklaces and bracelets, all made of gold. He had found his fortune.
data.teaser: What do you think Peter should do with his surprise fortune?

story.text: There once was a small tortoise who wanted to race the fastest animals in the forest. Everyone laughed, saying he was too slow. But the tortoise did not give up. On the day of the race, he walked steadily, never stopping to rest. The faster animals ran ahead but stopped along the way to rest and play. By the time they remembered the race, the tortoise had already crossed the finish line. The forest learned that slow and steady effort can win in the end.

levels.name: Number Recognition
levels.description: Recognizing, reading, and understanding the place value of numbers up to 100.

data.explanation: These are the first ten numbers. Each one represents a count of objects — 1 is a single item, 10 is a full group of ten.
data.practicePrompt: Try counting ten objects around you, one at a time, up to 10.

data.explanation: After 10, we start combining a ten with extra ones: 11 is 'ten and one', 12 is 'ten and two', and so on up to 20 (two full tens).
data.practicePrompt: Practice saying 11 through 20 out loud, noticing the 'ten and ___' pattern.

data.explanation: From here, numbers grow in groups of ten: 21, 22, 23... up to 30, then 31 to 40, then 41 to 50. Notice how the tens digit changes every ten numbers.
The same tens pattern continues all the way to 100, which is ten full groups of ten.
Every 2-digit number has a 'tens' digit and a 'ones' digit. In 47, the 4 means 4 tens (40) and the 7 means 7 ones. Together: 40 + 7 = 47.
data.practicePrompt: Break down these numbers into tens and ones: 35, 62, 89.

data.explanation: When you see a 2-digit number, read the tens digit first, then the ones digit — 53 is read as 'fifty-three', not 'five-three'.
data.practicePrompt: Practice reading these numbers the correct way: 16, 29, 53, 81.

lessons.title: Matching Numbers to Their Expanded Form

data.explanation: The expanded form of a number shows the value of each digit added together. 47 = 40 + 7. 68 = 60 + 8. 93 = 90 + 3.
data.practicePrompt: Try writing the expanded form of these numbers yourself: 52, 76, 39.

levels.name: Division
levels.description: Sharing quantities equally, including division word problems and remainders.

data.problem: 12 sticks shared equally among 4 friends — how many does each get?
steps: Division means sharing a total equally into groups.

data.problem: 72 mangoes shared among 3 people — how many each?
steps: Think: what number times 3 equals 72 (or close to it)?

data.problem: What is 45 ÷ 5?
Yasin has 35 marbles to share equally among 4 friends. How many each, with any left over?
steps: Think: what times 4 gets closest to 35 without going over?
4 x 8 = 32, which is the closest without exceeding 35.
Each friend gets 8, and 35 - 32 = 3 marbles are left over as the remainder.

practiceProblems.text: Robert splits 40 erasers between 7 classmates. How many each, and how many remain?

data.problem: Vincent gives 79 chocolates to 6 friends equally. How many does each friend get, and how many are left over?
steps: Think: 6 x 13 = 78, the closest without going over 79.
Each friend gets 13, and 79 - 78 = 1 chocolate is left over.

practiceProblems.text: If 74 people are grouped in 6s, how many full groups can be formed?

data.problem: A library has 567 books to place equally on 8 shelves. How many per shelf, and how many are left over?
steps: Think: what times 8 gets closest to 567 without going over?
567 - 560 = 7 books remain after filling 70 per shelf... but let's check more precisely: 8 x 70 = 560, remainder 7.
So each shelf gets about 70 books, with 7 left over.
